Reviewer Comment: The manuscript covers too many areas and the central scientific claims are not validated with sufficient rigor.
Author Response: We narrowed the NILM claims to what is validated: the protocol is documented in full, results are reported as mean +/- std over seeds with confidence intervals, an ablation isolates the architecture and loss contributions, baselines are re-implemented and trained under the identical protocol, and unseen-household, cross-dataset and adaptation experiments are added. Claims not supported by these experiments were removed (cross-dataset generalization, near-perfect state detection, literature-approximated baseline table). The hardware, web, security and forecasting parts are being revised separately.
Document Changes Made: Abstract, Introduction, NILM section (protocol, results, ablation, baselines, robustness, summary), Discussion, Limitations, Conclusion; web-technology and generic motivation text condensed.

Reviewer Comment: The NILM evaluation protocol and the meaning of cross-dataset generalization are unclear.
Author Response: We now give the complete experimental protocol in a dedicated table (Table 'Experimental protocol'): for every dataset the households, the training/validation/test split, the window counts (SustDataED2 1,416/303/304; REFIT 380,224/18,689/59,927; UK-DALE 11,610/2,488/2,488), the sampling interval (raw and used), the appliance set and the aggregate signal. We state explicitly that each dataset has its own independently trained model and that no cross-dataset training or fine-tuning is used in the main experiments.
Document Changes Made: Added Table 'Experimental protocol' and a 'Preprocessing' paragraph in Section 'Evaluation Datasets'; renamed 'Cross-Dataset Performance' to 'Multi-Dataset Performance'; abstract, introduction and Table 1 wording revised.

Reviewer Comment: Evaluation on separately trained models across SustDataED2, REFIT, and UK-DALE is multi-dataset validation, not necessarily cross-dataset generalization.
Author Response: We agree. The three-dataset evaluation is now described as multi-dataset validation of one architecture and training recipe. Genuine cross-household and cross-dataset evaluations are reported separately in the new Section 'Robustness to Unseen Households and Datasets'.
Document Changes Made: Section heading and text 'Multi-Dataset Performance'; abstract, introduction and Table 1 ('Multi-dataset validation; few-day EWC adaptation').

Reviewer Comment: The paper should add REFIT-to-UK-DALE, UK-DALE-to-REFIT, leave-one-house-out, unseen-house, zero-shot, and limited-adaptation evaluations.
Author Response: We added (i) per-house results on the unseen REFIT houses 18-21 (Table 'Per-house results'), (ii) leave-one-house-out training on five REFIT houses (mean gap to a model that has seen the house: about +1.0 W MAE and -0.02 F1; the gap is an upper bound because the held-out models were trained for fewer epochs), and (iii) a trained REFIT<->UK-DALE study on the five shared appliances with zero-shot testing (F1 retained 86-88% of the in-domain F1) and adaptation with the first 1, 3 and 7 days of the target household, compared with training from scratch. Within-dataset unseen-house evaluation is impossible for SustDataED2 and UK-DALE (single household) and this is stated.
Document Changes Made: New Section 'Robustness to Unseen Households and Datasets' with Tables 'Per-house results', 'Leave-one-house-out' and 'Zero-shot transfer and adaptation'.

Reviewer Comment: The methodological novelty of EDTCN and the device-type-weighted focal loss is not isolated.
Author Response: The component contributions are isolated in a controlled ablation (5 seeds, identical data and optimizer): architecture ladder (plain TCN, + residual, + exponential dilation with a 4-block and the 6-block receptive field) and loss ladder (MSE, MAE, MSE+MAE, standard focal, focal without type weights, type-weighted MSE, proposed loss). Dilation gives the main gain (MAE -11% on SustDataED2 and -12% on UK-DALE vs. the plain TCN); the proposed loss shifts the operating point toward higher recall at a small MAE cost. Quantization sensitivity is reported in the deployment section.
Document Changes Made: New Section 'Ablation Study' with Table 'Ablation study' and Table 'Effect of the device-type-weighted focal loss by usage type'.

Reviewer Comment: The mathematical formulation of the device-type-weighted focal loss is incomplete, including weight derivation, class weights, focusing parameter, normalization, and threshold selection.
Author Response: The loss is now stated explicitly (Eq. 'focal loss'): normalized error p = min(1, |y_hat - y| / max(|y|, 1 W)), L = mean over batch/time/appliances of w_type * p^gamma * (alpha*e^2 + (1-alpha)*e), with alpha = 0.7, gamma = 1.0, type weights A = B = 1.5 and C = 2.0 (fixed priors, not learned), the 1 W floor and the clipping that bound the factor, the normalization, and the role of the 15 W threshold (state metrics only, not in the loss). The previous equation omitted the floor and clipping.
Document Changes Made: Rewrote 'Regression Model' paragraph and Eq. (focal loss) in Section 'Training Strategy and Loss Functions'.

Reviewer Comment: It is unclear how focal loss, conventionally used for classification, is combined with appliance power regression.
Author Response: Clarified that the regression model has one output head per appliance and a pure regression objective; the 'focal' term is a bounded error-dependent modulation analogous to (1-p_t)^gamma in classification focal loss. State detection is obtained by thresholding the power estimate at 15 W. A separate classification network with weighted BCE is used only for the classification comparison.
Document Changes Made: Task Formulation paragraph and 'Regression Model' paragraph rewritten.

Reviewer Comment: A component-level statistical comparison is needed to demonstrate that EDTCN is more than a standard dilated TCN with empirical weighting.
Author Response: We provide mean +/- std over 5 seeds (3 for REFIT), block-bootstrap 95% intervals and paired block-bootstrap tests on identical test windows for every ablation variant and for the EDTCN versus the three baselines (all EDTCN-vs-baseline MAE differences p < 0.001). The comparison against the plain dilated-TCN-with-empirical-weighting question is answered by the loss ladder: the proposed weighting is not the source of the MAE gain, the dilated residual architecture is.
Document Changes Made: Ablation and baseline tables (with paired tests); overall-performance table with seeds and intervals.

Reviewer Comment: The real-time execution claim is unclear because inference takes approximately 111 seconds.
Author Response: We clarified what 'real-time' means for the NILM service: one inference processes a 512-step window (68.3 min of data at 8 s) in 101-123 s, i.e. 33-40 times faster than the data rate; with one inference per 15-minute reporting interval the result for an interval is available about 2 minutes after the interval ends. The text no longer presents this as sub-minute event detection. The previous throughput (7.9x) was computed from a 599-step window and has been corrected.
Document Changes Made: Hardware inference table (corrected speed-up, CPU duty), new paragraph 'Latency, duty cycle and energy', introduction wording.

Reviewer Comment: A 21-minute context window processed in 111 seconds may still introduce substantial output delay.
Author Response: A latency budget is now given (window buffering 68.3 min, inference 101-123 s, per-step 0.20-0.24 s, steady-state delay of an interval's result about 2 min). The network is almost causal (influence span t-4 ... t+256 steps measured by input perturbation), so each estimate depends on at most 32 s of future samples and an incremental implementation is architecturally possible; this is stated as not yet implemented.
Document Changes Made: New Table 'Latency budget' and text in 'Latency, duty cycle and energy'.

Reviewer Comment: CPU utilization approaches 100 percent, so concurrent metrology, FFT, display, tamper detection, communication, and storage must be evaluated.
The Discussion should be more argumentative and explain why the tested results were achieved.
Author Response: We added a Discussion subsection that argues why the results are as observed: temporal context (receptive field 31 -> 259 steps lowers MAE by 11-12%), residual connections needing dilation, the loss acting as an operating-point selector (MAE training underestimates energy; the weighted focal loss raises recall at a small MAE cost), and the dataset-dependent signal (closed-system aggregate on SustDataED2, unmetered load and overlapping signatures on REFIT/UK-DALE; states transfer better than amplitudes).
Document Changes Made: Section Discussion: new subsection 'Interpreting the NILM Results'; subsection 'Adaptation and the Cold-Start Problem' rewritten.

Reviewer Comment: The phrase without FPU support should clarify whether software-emulated floating-point preprocessing occurs before INT8 inference.
Author Response: Clarified: the convolutions run in INT8 integer arithmetic; the residual floating-point operations (input scaling, quantization scales, output de-quantization and thresholding) are executed by soft-float routines (-mfloat-abi=soft); they touch only 512 inputs and 512 x A outputs per window versus 3.8e8 multiply-accumulates in the network. Note: the INT8 models were rebuilt as true INT8 (the earlier files stored FP16 weights).

Reviewer Comment: The receptive-field calculation resulting in 127 timesteps should be derived explicitly.
Author Response: The receptive field is derived explicitly: R = 1 + (k_in - 1) + 2(K - 1) * sum(d_i) = 1 + 6 + 2*2*63 = 259 steps (kernel size K = 3 in the trained models), with a block-by-block table. An input-perturbation test on the deployed model confirms the influence span. The previous value of 127 steps (and K = 5) did not correspond to the trained checkpoints.
Document Changes Made: Architecture subsection, Table 'Receptive-field derivation', architecture figure and caption.

Reviewer Comment: The mapping of 127 timesteps to 21 minutes depends on a 10-second sampling interval and must be stated clearly.
Author Response: Stated explicitly: all datasets are resampled to 8 s, so the 259-step receptive field spans 34.5 minutes and the 512-step window 68.3 minutes; for other sampling intervals the span scales linearly (4.3 min at 1 s, 25.9 min at 6 s, 43.2 min at 10 s).
Document Changes Made: Architecture subsection, abstract.

Reviewer Comment: Dataset preprocessing needs details on missing values, resampling, normalization, synchronization, thresholds, activation filtering, periods, and voltage systems.
Author Response: Preprocessing is documented: resampling by averaging to an 8 s grid, forward-fill of gaps up to 7 samples, treatment of remaining gaps, timestamp synchronization of the SustDataED2 sensors, windowing (512 steps; stride 512, REFIT 256) and window-rejection rules, normalization with training statistics, ON/OFF threshold and absence of activation filtering, chronological/household splits, and handling of voltage (active power only). We also disclose that the SustDataED2 aggregate is the sum of the metered appliance channels.
Document Changes Made: 'Preprocessing' paragraph and dataset paragraphs in Section 'Evaluation Datasets'.

Reviewer Comment: The cloud LSTM forecasting module is weakly connected to the edge-NILM contribution.
A forecasting MAE of 12.70 W cannot be interpreted without scale, horizon, and baseline performance.
Cold-start adaptation and EWC are discussed, but the actual adaptation protocol is not fully described.
Author Response: The adaptation protocol is fully described: pretrained source model on the five shared appliances; which parameters are updated (output heads only, or all parameters, learning rates 3e-4 and 1e-4); amount of target data (first 1/3/7 days = 21/63/148 windows); chronological adaptation/validation/evaluation blocks with a guard window (REFIT windows overlap by 50%) and an exact-duplicate check (no overlap in any of the 24 configurations); EWC with a diagonal Fisher estimate on 640 source windows and a validation-selected penalty; 40 epochs, best validation checkpoint; adaptation is computed off-device (PC/cloud) and only the exported INT8 model is installed on the F1C200s.
Document Changes Made: Paragraph 'Cross-dataset transfer and adaptation protocol' in the Robustness section.

Reviewer Comment: The dishwasher MAE reduction from over 100 W to approximately 1 W after adaptation is unusually large and requires validation against leakage or overfitting.

The measured result is reported instead: the UK-DALE dishwasher has a zero-shot MAE of 18.1 W and 18.5-24.0 W after adaptation, i.e. rarely used appliances are not improved by a week of data. No overlap between adaptation, validation and evaluation windows was found.

Reviewer Comment: An ablation study is needed for dilated residual blocks, weighted focal loss, INT8 quantization, and compiler optimization.
Author Response: The contribution of each component is quantified: dilated residual blocks and the weighted focal loss in the ablation study (5 seeds), and INT8 quantization with true INT8 NCNN models evaluated on the complete test splits (REFIT 59,927, SustDataED2 304, UK-DALE 2,488 windows): with ACIQ clipping the regression MAE changes by -0.8%, +2.5% and 0.0%, and with the validation-selected mixed-precision model by at most +0.4%; classification macro-F1 is more sensitive (-0.13 to -0.18 for all-INT8 KL, within 0.035 for mixed precision). The NCNN INT8 tools skip 1-D convolutions, so the layers were expressed as exactly equivalent 2-D convolutions. The PNNX/compiler fusion is not separately ablated.
